title: What emergency contraception is
answer: Emergency contraception (EC) is a way to lower the chance of pregnancy after sex without protection, or when a method failed, for example a condom broke or pills were missed. There are two kinds: emergency contraceptive pills, sometimes called the morning-after pill, and a copper IUD put in by a trained provider. EC works best when used as soon as possible after sex.

title: How long after sex EC pills work
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills can be taken up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected sex. The sooner you take them, the better they work, so do not wait until the next morning if you can get them today. Even on day 4 or 5 they can still help. A copper IUD can also be fitted within 5 days.

title: How EC pills work
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by stopping or delaying the release of an egg from the ovary. If no egg is released while sperm are still alive in the body, fertilisation cannot happen. They do not work after an egg has been fertilised and they do not end a pregnancy that has already started.

title: EC is not abortion
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills are not abortion pills. They prevent pregnancy from starting, mainly by delaying the release of an egg. If a pregnancy has already begun, they do not end it and do not harm it. Using EC is a safe and responsible way to prevent an unplanned pregnancy after unprotected sex.

title: Taking EC when already pregnant
answer: If you are already pregnant, emergency contraceptive pills will not work, but they will not harm the pregnancy or the baby either. So if you took EC and later find out you were pregnant, there is no need to worry about damage from the pills. If your period is late, take a pregnancy test and talk to a health worker about your options and care.

title: Using EC more than once
answer: Yes, you can use emergency contraceptive pills more than once, and every time you need them. Using EC again is safe and does not cause infertility, cancer or other long-term harm. But if you often need EC, a regular method like pills, an injection, an implant or an IUD will protect you better. A health worker can help you choose.

title: Why EC is not for regular use
answer: Emergency contraception is safe, but it is meant as a backup, not an everyday method. It is less effective than regular methods like pills, injections, implants or IUDs, and using it often can make your bleeding irregular. If you have sex regularly, ask a health worker about a method that protects you all the time. Condoms also protect against STIs.

title: How effective EC pills are
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills greatly reduce the chance of pregnancy but do not remove it. For example, if 100 women had unprotected sex once in the middle of their cycle, about 8 might become pregnant without EC, but only about 1 or 2 with EC pills. They work best when taken as soon as possible. The copper IUD is even more effective as EC.

answer: Some people have mild side effects after taking emergency pills, such as nausea, stomach pain, tiredness, headache, sore breasts, dizziness or some spotting. title: Copper IUD as emergency contraception
answer: A copper IUD put into the womb within 5 days after unprotected sex is the most effective emergency contraception, preventing more than 99 out of 100 possible pregnancies. A trained provider at a health facility puts it in. It works even for people for whom pills may work less well. After that, it can stay in as a long-term method.

title: Most effective type of EC
answer: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception. Among pills, those containing ulipristal acetate are somewhat more effective than levonorgestrel pills, especially later in the 5-day window. All types work best when used as early as possible. Use whichever you can get quickly; any EC is better than none.

answer: There are three kinds of emergency contraceptive pills: progestin-only pills containing levonorgestrel (the most common), pills containing ulipristal acetate, and some ordinary combined pills used in a special way under a provider's guidance. title: What spermicides are
answer: Spermicides are products put deep into the vagina before sex to kill or stop sperm. They come as foam, gel, cream, tablets or film, and the most common one contains nonoxynol-9. Used alone, they are one of the least effective methods. They do not protect against HIV or other STIs.
